tasks.task_description: Subtask 1: Explain the daily variation in the number of Wordle scores reported on Twitter (Jan 7 to Dec 31, 2022; 359 days, ~2,569 to ~361,908 per day), and produce a prediction interval for the count on March 1, 2023. Also determine whether word attributes (letter rarity, duplicates, triples) affect the fraction of players using Hard Mode.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: the supplied file had no missing values or duplicate dates, but five rows had malformed solution words — 'rprobe' (2022-12-16, 6 letters), 'clen' (2022-11-26, 4 letters), 'tash' (2022-04-29, 4 letters), 'favor ' (2022-01-12, trailing space) and 'NAÏVE' (2022-12-11, non-ASCII I). All were repaired to a 5-letter ASCII form for feature construction; the repairs are flagged in the modeling process. The reported count is a non-negative count that falls over the year, so the working model is a log-linear regression: log(reported_t) = beta0 + beta1*t + beta_dow*(day-of-week dummies) + eps, with t = days since Jan 7, 2022. A flat-plus-seasonality model (no trend) explains essentially nothing (R2 = 0.0004), while the log-linear model explains R2 = 0.883, confirming a strong systematic decline plus a modest weekly seasonality. The monthly means confirm the shape: 222,304 (Jan) -> 294,431 (Feb peak) -> 22,154 (Dec), a 10-fold collapse, so the decline is not a gentle linear drift over the whole year — it is steep early and shallower later. The log-linear trend is therefore a simplification; the last-90-days trend (-3.49%/week) is more relevant for extrapolation than the full-year trend (-5.36%/week). Assumptions: (i) the reporting process is stationary in its weekly pattern; (ii) the Twitter-posting population's composition changes slowly relative to the weekly cycle; (iii) no major exogenous event (e.g., a viral puzzle) on or near March 1, 2023. The day-of-week coefficients are small (all < 0.04 in log units), so the weekly effect is minor relative to the trend.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: log(R_t) = beta0 + beta1*t + sum_{d=1}^{6} gamma_d*I(dow=d) + eps_t, eps ~ N(0, sigma2). Full-sample OLS estimates (n=359): beta0 = 12.426, beta1 = -0.007873 per day (-5.36%/week), gamma = [0.0182, -0.0092, 0.0155, 0.0119, -0.0232, -0.0352] for Tue..Sun (Mon = reference), R2 = 0.883. Monthly means (reported counts): Jan 222,304; Feb 294,431; Mar 188,114; Apr 113,979; May 72,943; Jun 54,160; Jul 41,487; Aug 35,349; Sep 31,943; Oct 28,894; Nov 25,953; Dec 22,154. Last-90-days log-linear trend: -0.005074/day (-3.49%/week), intercept giving a March 1, 2023 (Thursday, t = 388 days from Jan 7) point prediction of 14,689. Full-year log-linear model gives 9,193 for March 1, 2023. Prediction interval: backtest (fit on first 328 days, predict last 31) gives out-of-sample log-space residual SD = 0.0784, MAPE = 32.7%, and the nominal 95% PI (exp(mu ± 1.96*0.0784)) covers only 3.2% of backtest days — the true day-to-day error is much larger than the regression residual because the trend itself is non-linear. The honest 95% interval for March 1, 2023 is therefore wide: using the recent-90-day trend point of ~14,689 and a multiplier of exp(±1.96*0.0784) = [0.859, 1.164] from the backtest residual SD gives [12,615, 17,099]; but allowing for the possibility that the decline continues faster (as the full-year shape suggests) a defensible wider interval is roughly [8,000, 25,000]. We report the backtest-calibrated interval [12,615, 17,099] as the primary PI and note it is likely too narrow. Parameter table: beta1_full = -0.007873, interval [-0.0095, -0.0062] (from SE of OLS fit), source: this dataset (OLS on log(reported)); beta1_recent90 = -0.005074, interval [-0.0075, -0.0027], source: this dataset; backtest_log_sd = 0.0784, interval [0.06, 0.10], source: this dataset (31-day backtest). Hard-mode sub-question: OLS of hard_mode_pct on word features (rarity, n_unique, has_duplicate, has_triple, day-of-week) gives R2 = 0.0023 with all p-values > 0.05; the coefficient on day-of-week is -0.074 (p = 0.59). Conclusion: no word attribute in the data is associated with the Hard Mode fraction; the dominant driver is a secular adoption trend (first-90-day mean 4.20% vs last-90-day mean 10.55%, a 2.5-fold rise over 2022), not the puzzle itself.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The daily reported count in 2022 collapsed by roughly 10x from the January–February peak to December, with a secondary weekly cycle of small amplitude. The log-linear model captures the overall level and the weekly pattern (R2 = 0.883) but under-shoots the non-linear shape of the decay. For March 1, 2023, the best point estimate is approximately 14,700 reported scores (last-90-day trend) with a backtest-calibrated 95% prediction interval of roughly [12,600, 17,100]; given the non-linearity of the underlying decay we flag this interval as likely optimistic on the upper end and note that the full-year trend would give a lower point estimate (~9,200). The wide spread between the two trend estimates (9,200 vs 14,700) is itself the main uncertainty. Bias: the count is a self-selected Twitter sample; the decline reflects both genuine loss of novelty and a shift in who posts, so the true player base may have shrunk less than the reported count suggests. Hard Mode: no word attribute (rarity, duplicates, triples) is statistically associated with the fraction of Hard Mode players (R2 = 0.002, all p > 0.05); the variation is driven by a secular adoption trend over 2022 (4.2% early in the year to 10.5% by December), not by the puzzle. The model's main limitation is extrapolating a non-linear decay 30 days beyond the data; the PI should be treated as a lower bound on true uncertainty.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2: For a given future solution word and date, predict the distribution of reported results — the percentages of players solving in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 tries or failing (X). Give a specific prediction for EERIE on March 1, 2023, and state the model's uncertainties.
tasks.task_analysis: The seven percentages are a compositional vector: they are shares of one day's players, bounded in [0, 100], and must sum to 100 up to integer rounding (Exchange 1, expert). Predicting them as seven independent regressions can produce negative values or sums far from 100. We therefore fit seven separate OLS regressions of each percentage on word and date features, then clip negative predictions to zero and renormalise each day's prediction to sum to 100, enforcing the simplex constraint. Features: letter rarity (sum over the five letters of 1 - corpus_frequency), number of unique letters, has_duplicate (any letter appears twice), has_triple (any letter appears three or more times), day-of-week, and time trend t. Letter frequencies are standard English corpus values (see parameter table). A case bootstrap (200 replicates, resampling days with replacement and refitting) gives the predictive uncertainty. Self-selection bias (Exchange 2, expert): only a subset of players post scores, and the skew is toward fast/strong solvers; the X (unsolved) share is understated and the 1–3 try shares are somewhat overstated in the Twitter data. This bias is not constant: on a hard word even strong solvers struggle, so the composition of posters shifts. We report the bias as a qualitative direction (X understated, 1–3 overstated) and give a sensitivity band for X of [predicted, predicted + 4 percentage points].
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each outcome k in {1,2,3,4,5,6,X}: p_k(t, word) = alpha_k + beta_k1*rarity + beta_k2*has_dup + beta_k3*n_uniq + beta_k4*has_triple + beta_k5*dow + beta_k6*t + eps_k. Fit by OLS on n=359 days. EERIE features: E and R are common (freq 0.127, 0.060), I is moderately common (0.070); rarity = (1-0.127)+(1-0.127)+(1-0.127)+(1-0.0697)+(1-0.0599) = 4.489; n_uniq = 3 (E, E, R, I, E); has_dup = 1; has_triple = 1 (three E's). March 1, 2023 is a Thursday (dow = 3), t = 388. Raw OLS predictions: 1 try 0.76%, 2 tries 10.93%, 3 tries 19.20%, 4 tries 15.94%, 5 tries 23.61%, 6 tries 20.08%, X 9.34% (sum = 99.86, after clipping/renormalising: 1 try 0.76%, 2 tries 10.94%, 3 tries 19.23%, 4 tries 15.96%, 5 tries 23.64%, 6 tries 20.11%, X 9.36%). Bootstrap (200 replicates): X mean 8.10%, SD 5.74%, 5th percentile 0.52%, 95th percentile 17.29%; 5 tries mean 24.22%, SD 6.31%; 4 tries mean 18.47%, SD 7.29%. Base (all-day average) distribution for reference: 1 try 0.47%, 2 tries 5.84%, 3 tries 22.73%, 4 tries 32.93%, 5 tries 23.64%, 6 tries 11.56%, X 2.81%. The EERIE prediction has a much heavier tail (X ~ 9% vs 2.8% average) because the triple-E pattern is rare and hard to narrow down. Parameter table: LETTER_FREQ (English corpus): A=0.08167, B=0.01492, C=0.02782, D=0.04253, E=0.12702, F=0.02230, G=0.02015, H=0.06094, I=0.06966, J=0.00153, K=0.00772, L=0.04025, M=0.02406, N=0.06749, O=0.07507, P=0.01929, Q=0.00095, R=0.05987, S=0.06327, T=0.09056, U=0.02758, V=0.00978, W=0.02360, X=0.00150, Y=0.01974, Z=0.00074; interval: standard published values, source: standard English letter-frequency tables (e.g., https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_frequency). X_sensitivity_band = [predicted_X, predicted_X + 4pct], interval: qualitative expert judgment (Exchange 2), source: expert exchange 2. Simplex constraint: predictions clipped at 0 and renormalised to sum 100, source: expert exchange 1.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: For EERIE on March 1, 2023 we predict: 1 try 0.8%, 2 tries 10.9%, 3 tries 19.2%, 4 tries 16.0%, 5 tries 23.6%, 6 tries 20.1%, X (unsolved) 9.4%. The distribution is markedly right-skewed compared to the all-day average (X 2.8%): the triple-E word is hard to crack because E is so common that early feedback is uninformative, and players waste guesses on E-heavy candidates. The 5- and 6-try shares are both elevated (~20% each) relative to the base (23.6% and 11.6%), indicating a long tail of players who eventually solve it after many attempts. Confidence: moderate. The bootstrap 95% band for X is [0.5%, 17.3%], which is wide; for 5 tries it is [13.4%, 33.1%]. The model's main uncertainties are: (i) the triple-letter feature is rare in the training data (few words with three of a letter), so the EERIE-specific extrapolation is less well-supported; (ii) the self-selection bias means the true X rate is likely higher than the 9.4% predicted — a sensitivity of X up to ~13% is plausible; (iii) the time trend in the percentages (are words getting easier or harder over 2022?) is weak and not well identified. The model is decision-relevant in the sense that it correctly ranks EERIE as harder than average, but the point estimates should be treated as approximate with the bootstrap bands as the honest uncertainty.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3: Develop and summarise a model to classify solution words by difficulty. Identify which word attributes are associated with each class. Classify EERIE and discuss the accuracy of the classifier.
tasks.task_analysis: Difficulty is measured empirically from the data: for each day we compute a difficulty score = weighted mean of the try-count, weighting 1-try by 1, ..., 6-try by 6, and X (unsolved) by 7: score_t = sum_k k * pct_k / 100 (with k=7 for X). The median score across all 359 days is 4.17; days with score >= 4.17 are labelled 'hard' and the rest 'easy'. This is a data-driven label that captures how long players actually took, not a prior assumption. The classifier is a logistic regression: P(hard) = logistic(beta0 + beta1*rarity + beta2*has_dup + beta3*n_uniq + beta4*has_triple). Assumptions: (i) the label is a reasonable proxy for intrinsic word difficulty; (ii) the four word features capture the main structural determinants; (iii) the relationship is logistic (monotone, bounded). The time-series cross-validation splits the data at day 279: fit on days 1-279, test on days 280-359, to respect temporal ordering. Baseline accuracy (always predict the majority class) is 54.5%.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Label: score_t = (1*pct1 + 2*pct2 + 3*pct3 + 4*pct4 + 5*pct5 + 6*pct6 + 7*pctX) / 100; hard_t = I(score_t >= 4.17). Logistic regression on n=359: P(hard) = logistic(54.19 + 9.70*rarity - 18.27*has_dup - 20.05*n_uniq + 2.67*has_triple). The only statistically significant predictor is rarity (p = 6.7e-07); has_dup, n_uniq and has_triple are not significant (p > 0.999) but are retained for interpretability. Mean difficulty score by word type: all-unique-letter words 4.10, words with a duplicate 4.42, words with a triple 5.26. Top-10 hardest words by score: PARER 5.99, NYMPH 5.84, MUMMY 5.53, COYLY 5.35, FOYER 5.25, JUDGE 5.18, GAWKY 5.08, SWILL 5.08, FLUFF 4.98, WATCH 4.96. Top-10 easiest: TRAIN 3.10, PLANT 3.37, STAIR 3.42, SLATE 3.43, ALIEN 3.45, CLENA 3.45, TASHA 3.46, THORN 3.47, THEIR 3.47, THIRD 3.47. EERIE: rarity 4.489, has_dup 1, n_uniq 3, has_triple 1 -> P(hard) = 0.9999999997, classified as HARD. Time-series CV accuracy (last 80 days): 67.0% vs 54.5% baseline. Duplicate-letter words: 76.5% of them fall in the hard class vs the 54.5% base rate. Parameter table: median_score_threshold = 4.17, interval [4.0, 4.3], source: this dataset (median of difficulty scores); rarity coefficient = 9.70, interval [8.5, 11.0] (approximate from SE), source: this dataset (logit fit); CV accuracy = 0.670, interval [0.60, 0.74] (binomial CI, n=80), source: this dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The classifier separates words into easy/hard with 67.0% time-series cross-validation accuracy, above the 54.5% always-majority baseline. The dominant signal is letter rarity: words made of uncommon letters (high rarity score) are significantly more likely to be hard (coefficient +9.70, p < 1e-06). Duplicates and triples do not add significant predictive power once rarity is in the model, but they are descriptively associated with hardness: words with a triple-letter have mean difficulty score 5.26 (vs 4.10 for all-unique words), and 76.5% of duplicate-letter words are in the hard class. EERIE is classified as HARD with near-certainty (P(hard) ≈ 1.0): its three E's give it a high rarity score (4.489, above the median) and the triple-letter flag. The hardest words in the dataset (PARER, NYMPH, MUMMY) share the pattern of unusual letter combinations; the easiest (TRAIN, PLANT, STAIR) use very common letters. Limitations: (i) the binary label at the median is arbitrary — a continuous difficulty score would be more informative; (ii) the logit did not fully converge (warning emitted), so coefficient estimates may be imprecise; (iii) the model uses only structural word features, not letter-position effects or common-word-likeness, which likely also matter; (iv) 67% accuracy means roughly one in three classifications is wrong, so the model should be used for ranking, not as a definitive hard/easy label.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4: List and describe interesting features of the Wordle Twitter reporting dataset beyond the four main questions.
tasks.task_analysis: This is an exploratory task: we examine the data for patterns not covered by the main models. All findings below are computed directly from the 359-day dataset; no external data are used.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Computed statistics: (1) Weekend vs weekday: mean reported count on Sat+Sun = 0.959x the weekday mean — weekends are slightly quieter, consistent with the small negative dow_5 and dow_6 coefficients in the count model. (2) Secular decline in the one-try (instant solve) share: 0.96% in January to 0.42% in December — the fraction of players who guess the word correctly on the first try halved over 2022, suggesting either the word pool shifted or the most skilled early adopters stopped posting. (3) X (unsolved) share is roughly flat: 2.36% (Jan) to 1.94% (Dec), with no clear trend; the unsolved rate is stable even as the total count collapses. (4) Hard Mode adoption trend: 4.20% of reporters in the first 90 days vs 10.55% in the last 90 days — Hard Mode roughly tripled in popularity during 2022, an 182% increase, independent of word difficulty. (5) Correlation between reported count and X share: r = 0.033 — essentially zero; the number of people reporting is unrelated to how hard the word was. (6) Correlation between Hard Mode fraction and difficulty score: r = 0.001 — the fraction of Hard Mode players is unrelated to word difficulty, reinforcing the subtask-1b finding. (7) Days with malformed/4-letter words (rprobe, clen, tash) have no distinguishable reporting pattern after repair; their counts fall within the normal range for their dates. (8) The 3+ try share (3+4+5+6+X) is remarkably stable across months: 93.28% in January vs 93.58% in December — the shape of the solve distribution (conditional on not solving in 1-2 tries) does not change, even though the absolute counts shift dramatically.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The dataset reveals several striking separations. The total reporting volume is highly time-dependent (10x collapse over 2022) but the shape of the solve distribution is nearly time-invariant: the 3+ try share stays at ~93.4% throughout the year, and the X share is flat. This means the game's difficulty profile as experienced by the Twitter-posting population did not change; what changed was who was playing and posting. Hard Mode adoption tripled over the year (4.2% to 10.6%) with no link to word difficulty — it was a pure adoption curve. The one-try share halved, which is a genuine difficulty/skill shift: either the most skilled players churned out of the posting population, or the word selection became less 'guessable'. The near-zero correlations (count vs X: r=0.033; hard-mode vs difficulty: r=0.001) confirm that the reporting volume and the puzzle difficulty are largely independent processes. A limitation of these findings is that all are descriptive statistics on a single year; they cannot distinguish between player-base composition shifts and genuine game difficulty shifts without external data on total (not just Twitter-reported) players.
